They are: The offspring of a sin offering; the substitute for a sin offering; a sin offering whose owner died; a sin offering whose owner achieved atonement with another sin offering, when the original sin offering was lost or stolen and later recovered; and a sin offering whose year has passed. The mishna continues the discussion of the distinction between individual and communal offerings.

mishnayos.summary: Some animals may never be brought on the mizbe'ach, and if even one gets mixed with others, all of them become forbidden. The mishnah lists them, like an animal set aside for avodah zarah or one that was worshipped.

chunks.en: All animals that are forbidden on the mizbe'ach

an animal used for a terrible sin, in two ways,

words.note: An animal used for a very bad, forbidden act.

chunks.en: one set aside for avodah zarah, one that was worshipped,

mishnayos.summary: An animal given as payment for a forbidden act may not be brought as a korban. The mishnah explains which payment counts, and Rebbi and the Sages argue about one case.

mishnayos.summary: An animal given in exchange for a dog may not be brought as a korban, even when partners divide their animals. The Torah forbids only these two cases, and the babies of these animals are allowed.

chunks.en: What is the price of a dog?
If someone says to his friend,
"Here is this lamb
in place of this dog."
And also two partners who divided their animals:
one took ten lambs,
and the other took nine and a dog.
The ones taken in place of the dog
are forbidden; the ones with the dog are allowed.
But a dog's payment and the price of a zonah
are allowed,
as it says,
"both of them": two, and not four.
Their babies are allowed,
as it says "them,"
and not their babies.

mishnayos.summary: If the forbidden payment was money, it may be used to buy a korban, but wine, oil and flour are forbidden. Holy things given are still allowed, but birds become forbidden, as the Torah says "for any vow."

chunks.en: If he gave her money,
it is allowed.
Wine, oil,
flour, and anything like these
that is brought on the mizbe'ach,
is forbidden. If he gave her holy things,
they are allowed.
Birds are forbidden.
We might have thought:
If holy animals,
which a blemish makes unfit,
do not become a forbidden payment or price,
then birds, which a blemish does not make unfit,
shouldn't it make sense that
payment and price should not take hold on them?
So the Torah says:
"For any vow,"
to include birds.

chunks.en: Hekdesh for fixing the Beis HaMikdash takes hold on everything,

chunks.en: and using what grows from them is me'ilah,
chunks.st: and one is liable to bring a guilt offering and pay an additional payment of one-fifth for misuse of consecrated property, not only for the items themselves, but for their by-products, e.g., milk of a consecrated animal or eggs of a consecrated chicken;

words.note: Using something holy for yourself.

chunks.en: and the Kohanim get no use from them.
chunks.st: and there is no benefit for the owner from items consecrated for Temple maintenance, in contrast to some animals consecrated for the altar, e.g., a peace offering, from which there is benefit for the owner.

mishnayos.stIntro: While the previous mishna enumerated differences between consecration for the altar and consecration for Temple maintenance, this mishna enumerates halakhot that apply to both.

mishnayos.summary: Some things that may not be used are buried, like the hair of a nazir, a firstborn donkey, and meat cooked in milk. Rabbi Shimon says plain animals shechted in the Beis HaMikdash courtyard are burned.

chunks.en: These are the things that are buried:
Korban animals whose babies were born not alive
are buried. If it gave birth to the afterbirth,
it is buried. An ox that beis din put to death,
and the calf of the egla arufah,

words.note: The egla arufah, a calf used in a special ceremony when a killer is not known.

chunks.en: and the birds of a metzora,

words.note: A person with tzaraas, a skin sickness sent as a punishment.

chunks.en: the hair of a nazir,

words.note: A person who promised not to drink wine or cut his hair.

chunks.en: the firstborn of a donkey,
meat cooked in milk,
and plain animals shechted in the courtyard.

words.note: The Azarah, the yard of the Beis HaMikdash.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon says:
Plain animals shechted in the courtyard
are burned, and so is a wild animal shechted in the courtyard.

mishnayos.summary: Some forbidden things are burned, like chametz on Pesach and tamei terumah. Food of orlah and kilayim is burned, while drinks are buried, and we may light a fire with tamei terumah bread and oil.

mishnayos.summary: Korbanos shechted with a wrong plan about their time or place are burned. Rabbi Yehudah and the Sages argue about some cases, and about whether someone may burn what is supposed to be buried.

chunks.en: All korbanos that were shechted with a plan to be outside
their time or outside their place
are burned.
An asham talui,

words.note: An asham brought when a person is not sure if he sinned.

chunks.en: is burned. Rabbi Yehudah says:

chunks.he: יִקָּבֵר. חַטַּאת הָעוֹף הַבָּאָה עַל סָפֵק,
chunks.en: It is buried. A bird chatas brought because of a doubt
is burned. Rabbi Yehudah says:
He throws it into the water channel.

words.note: A stream of water that ran through the courtyard.

chunks.en: Everything that is burned may not be buried,
and everything that is buried may not be burned.
Rabbi Yehudah says:
If he wants to be strict with
himself and burn what is supposed to be buried,
he may. They said to him:
It is not allowed to change.
